What is the resultant force on the car at t = 10 s?
A
0
B
1500 N
C
2000 N
D
4000 N

hints: Look at where $t = 10\text{ s}$ sits on the $p$ against $t$ graph: it is on the straight rising section from $t = 0$ to $t = 20\text{ s}$ where $p$ goes from $1 \times 10^4$ to $4 \times 10^4\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$.
Connect the graph to physics: resultant force equals rate of change of momentum, $F = \Delta p/\Delta t$, so you need the gradient of that straight section.
Work out $\Delta p$ over the full $0$ to $20\text{ s}$ straight line and divide by $20\text{ s}$ to get the constant force acting at $10\text{ s}$.
walkthrough: Identify the relevant part of the graph: $t = 10\text{ s}$ lies in the first straight-line section from $t = 0$ to $t = 20\text{ s}$.
State the governing rule: resultant force is the gradient of a momentum-time graph, $F = \Delta p / \Delta t$.
Find the change in momentum over that section: $\Delta p = (4 - 1) \times 10^4 = 3.0 \times 10^4\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ with $\Delta t = 20 - 0 = 20\text{ s}$.
Substitute to find the gradient: $F = (3.0 \times 10^4)/20 = 1500\text{ kg m s}^{-2} = 1500\text{ N}$.
Since the section is straight, this gradient and force are constant, so this is the force at $t = 10\text{ s}$. This is option B.

A.explanation: Zero force means zero gradient, which occurs on the flat section from $t = 20\text{ s}$ to $50\text{ s}$, not at $t = 10\text{ s}$ where $p$ is increasing.

B.explanation: The gradient from $0$ to $20\text{ s}$ is $(3 \times 10^4)/(20) = 1500\text{ N}$, which equals the resultant force at $t = 10\text{ s}$.

C.explanation: This uses $4 \times 10^4/20$ and ignores that $p$ starts at $1 \times 10^4\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$, so the change is only $3 \times 10^4\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$.

D.explanation: This uses $4 \times 10^4/10$ at $t = 10\text{ s}$, which confuses the $p$ value with the change in $p$ and the time interval with the instant.
